title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive in an automated licence-plate recognition system, and it happened at the point where a machine-generated alert meets a human decision to stop someone. The system matched a plate to a stolen-vehicle record on the strength of a single misread character, and the match was acted on as grounds for a felony stop. The failure mode is a model asserting a match as fact when the underlying read was wrong, with no verification step standing between the alert and the drawn weapon.

Catching this would not have required better software alone. It would have required the deputy to confirm the plate against the record before treating the alert as sufficient cause, which is what the vendor itself says should happen. The reported contributing factor, an illegal tinted plate cover, is a condition the system was not built to see through, and the facts do not establish whether the misread was caused by the cover, by the reader, or by both.

What is not established is whether the detention was lawful or whether the deputy's conduct will be reviewed by anyone outside the sheriff's office, which has already called it reasonable. The account of the misread rests on the sheriff's office's own explanation, and no independent finding has been reported.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, of York County, South Carolina, was detained at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the error and called the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
